summary.text: Take \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and choose an arbitrarily large prime \(p\) (in particular, \(p\ge 81\)); among integers at most \(p\), only \(1\) and \(p\) have all prime factors drawn from \(\{p\}\), so \(a(p)\le2\), whereas \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the proposed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ is a prime factor of }n\}.
\]
(As usual, the set of prime factors of \(1\) is empty.) We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]
Here powers with real exponents are interpreted as real powers, and the natural number \(a(n)\) is viewed as a real number in the displayed inequality.

The key observation is that \(a(n)\) stays bounded along the infinite sequence of prime inputs. More precisely, if \(p\) is prime, then
\[
a(p)\le 2.
\]
Indeed, the only prime factor of \(p\) is \(p\) itself. Consider an integer \(k\) counted by \(a(p)\). Thus \(1\le k\le p\), and every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to the singleton set \(\{p\}\). If \(k=1\), it is one of the two possible values. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). Since every prime factor of \(k\) must be a prime factor of \(p\), we have \(q=p\), and hence \(p\mid k\). But \(k\) is positive and \(k\le p\), so the divisibility \(p\mid k\) forces \(k=p\). Consequently every integer counted by \(a(p)\) lies in \(\{1,p\}\), proving \(a(p)\le2\). In fact both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted, so \(a(p)=2\), although only the upper bound is needed.

We also record the elementary numerical estimate
\[
e^4<81.
\]
One standard way to see the estimate used here is that \(e<3\). For example, from the exponential series,
\[
e=1+1+\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\frac1{m!}.
\]
For \(m\ge2\), one has \(m!\ge2^{m-1}\), and at least one of these inequalities is strict, so
\[
\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\frac1{m!}
 <\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\frac1{2^{m-1}}=1.
\]
Thus \(e<3\), and raising positive numbers to the fourth power gives
\[
e^4<3^4=81.
\]
Equivalently, \(\exp(4)<81\).

It follows that for every positive integer \(p\ge81\),
\[
4<\log p.
\]
Indeed,
\[
\exp(4)<81\le p=\exp(\log p),
\]
where the last equality holds because \(p>0\). Since the exponential function is strictly increasing, comparison of the two exponentials yields \(4<\log p\).

Taking positive square roots preserves this strict inequality. Since \(\sqrt4=2\), we therefore obtain, for every \(p\ge81\),
\[
2<\sqrt{\log p}=(\log p)^{1/2}.
\]

We now suppose, for contradiction, that the conjectured eventual lower bound holds. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There is then some \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}=(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose a prime \(p\) at least as large as both \(N\) and \(81\). Such a prime exists because primes are arbitrarily large. For completeness, given any bound \(B\), take a prime divisor \(p\) of \((B+1)!+1\). If \(p\le B+1\), then \(p\) divides \((B+1)!\), while by construction it also divides \((B+1)!+1\); it would then divide their difference \(1\), which is impossible. Hence \(p>B+1>B\). Applying this with \(B=\max\{N,81\}\) supplies the required prime.

Since \(p\ge N\), the asserted lower bound gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
Since \(p\) is prime, the prime-input observation gives
\[
a(p)\le2.
\]
On the other hand, since \(p\ge81\), the logarithmic estimate gives
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}.
\]
Combining these three inequalities produces
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)\le2,
\]
a contradiction.

Therefore the proposed statement is false. In particular, already for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), no threshold \(N\) can make \(a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1/2}\) hold for every \(n\ge N\): every sufficiently large prime is a counterexample.
